subject: copper needles orbit
title: What If We Put 480 Million Needles in Orbit? In 1963 America Did

scenes.text: What if we wrapped Earth in a ring of copper needles? In 1963, America did.
In the Cold War, the military wanted radio links that couldn't be jammed or cut. MIT's Lincoln Laboratory proposed an artificial radio mirror in space.
The plan: 480 million copper needles, each 1.8 centimetres long and thinner than a hair, spread in a belt about 3,500 kilometres up.
A first attempt in 1961 failed. The second, in 1963, worked: voices were bounced off the needles between California and Massachusetts.
Astronomers around the world were furious. And Telstar, the first modern communications satellite, was already flying. The belt was never repeated.
Not all the needles spread out as planned. Fifty years later, NASA still counted 46 clumps of them circling the Earth.

description:
What if we gave Earth an artificial ring of metal? Project West Ford did: MIT's Lincoln Laboratory launched 480 million hair-thin copper needles, each 1.8 centimetres long, to act as a radio reflector about 3,500 kilometres up.
After a failed first try in 1961, the 1963 launch worked and voice was relayed between California and Massachusetts. Astronomers protested strongly, and communications satellites such as Telstar made the idea obsolete. Only part of the needles dispersed properly; in 2013 NASA reported 46 clumps still in orbit.
What should we run through next?
thumbnail_text: WHAT IF EARTH HAD A NEEDLE RING?
first_comment: At first the belt carried about 20 kilobits a second; four months later it was down to 100 bits. Brilliant or reckless, and what should we run through next?
